content.text: Cyber Jurisprudence and Indian Taxation Architecture: IT Act, Cyber Security, Direct Taxes, and the GST Framework

Contemporary public administration requires sound knowledge of cyber laws to regulate cyberspace, investigate digital crimes, and manage data sovereignty, alongside fiscal tax laws governing resource mobilization through direct taxation (Income Tax and Corporate Tax under the Income Tax Act, 1961) and indirect taxation under the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime.
1. The Information Technology Act, 2000 & Cyber Crimes

Enacted pursuant to the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce (1996), the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000 provides legal recognition to electronic transactions, digital signatures, and e-governance, while criminalizing offenses in cyberspace:

content.caption: Key Offenses Penalized under the Information Technology Act, 2000
rows: Section 43 & 43A
Unauthorized access to computer systems, data theft, virus introduction; failure to protect sensitive personal data by corporations.
Civil liability; compensation to the victim; mandates implementation of reasonable security practices by corporate entities.
Section 66
Computer-related offenses (Hacking with fraudulent intent).
Imprisonment up to 3 years or fine up to ₹5 lakh or both.
Section 66A
Punishment for sending offensive messages through communication services.
Declared UNCONSTITUTIONAL and struck down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) for violating freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) and being overly vague.
Section 66C & 66D
Identity theft, spoofing, and cheating by personation using computer resources (phishing).
Imprisonment up to 3 years and fine up to ₹1 lakh.
Section 66E
Violation of privacy (capturing, publishing images of private body parts without consent).
Imprisonment up to 3 years or fine up to ₹2 lakh.
Section 66F
Cyber Terrorism (threatening national sovereignty, unity, integrity, or critical information infrastructure).
Imprisonment which may extend to imprisonment for life (cognizable and non-bailable).
Section 67, 67A, 67B
Publishing or transmitting obscene material, sexually explicit acts, or child pornography in electronic form.
Severe penalties; up to 5 years imprisonment on first conviction, 7 years on subsequent conviction.
Section 69 & 69A
Powers of Central Government to intercept, decrypt, or block public access to information in the interest of national sovereignty, defense, or public order.
Upheld in Shreya Singhal (2015) subject to strict procedural safeguards and written reasoned orders.

content.text: 2. Cyber Security Architecture & Jurisdictional Challenges in Cyber Crimes

items: National Cyber Security Policy & Agencies: (1) CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team under Section 70B IT Act) serving as the national nodal agency for incident response; (2) NCIIPC (National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre under Section 70A) protecting designated sectors like banking, power grids, and defense; (3) I4C (Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre) operating the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (1930 emergency helpline).

Jurisdictional Dilemmas: Cyberspace is borderless, anonymous, and ephemeral, challenging traditional territorial criminal jurisdiction (Section 177 CrPC). Section 75 of the IT Act confers extra-territorial jurisdiction if the offense involves a computer system located in India; however, investigating cross-border cybercrimes faces severe handicaps: foreign server locations (e.g., VPNs, dark web, bulletproof hosting), delays in Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLAT), encrypted messaging platforms refusing metadata sharing, and conflicting privacy standards across jurisdictions.

content.text: 3. Direct Tax Laws: Income Tax, Corporate Tax, and Abolition of Wealth Tax
Direct taxation in India is administered by the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) under the Ministry of Finance pursuant to the Income Tax Act, 1961:

content.caption: Structure of Direct Taxes in India
rows: Personal Income Tax
Income Tax Act, 1961

Progressive progressive tax levied on total income across five statutory heads: (1) Salaries, (2) Income from House Property, (3) Profits and Gains of Business/Profession, (4) Capital Gains, and (5) Income from Other Sources.
Introduction of Simplified New Tax Regime (Section 115BAC) with lower slab rates but fewer exemptions; faceless assessment and faceless appeal systems to minimize corruption and harassment.
Corporate Income Tax
Income Tax Act, 1961
Tax levied on net profits earned by domestic companies and foreign corporations operating in India.

Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 slashed base corporate tax for existing domestic companies from 30% to 22% (Section 115BAA), and for new manufacturing firms to 15% (Section 115BAB), positioning India competitively in global supply chains.
Wealth Tax (Abolished)
Wealth Tax Act, 1957
Historically levied at 1% on net wealth exceeding ₹30 lakh on non-productive physical assets (jewellery, yachts, urban land).
Abolished in Union Budget 2015–16 due to high administrative compliance costs and negligible revenue yields (replaced with an additional 2% surcharge on super-rich individuals earning >₹1 crore).
Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT)
Section 115JB of Income Tax Act
Levied at 15% on book profits of 'zero-tax companies' that generate huge commercial accounting profits but pay zero tax using exemptions.
Prevents corporate tax avoidance while maintaining investment incentives.

content.text: 4. Indirect Tax Overhaul: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) Architecture

Enacted through the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 and implemented on July 1, 2017 ('One Nation, One Tax, One Market'), GST replaced a cascade of 17 central and state indirect levies (Excise, Service Tax, State VAT, Entry Tax, Luxury Tax):

items: Dual GST Model: Concurrently levied by the Centre and States on a common base: (1) Central GST (CGST) and State GST (SGST) on intra-state supplies; (2) Integrated GST (IGST) levied by the Centre under Article 269A on inter-state supplies and imports, apportioned between Centre and consuming State.

Destination-Based Consumption Tax: Unlike previous origin-based manufacturing excises, GST taxes value addition at each stage and accrues revenue to the consuming State, benefiting net consumer states.
Input Tax Credit (ITC): Seamless cross-utilization of taxes paid on input goods and services against output tax liability, eliminating the cascading 'tax-on-tax' phenomenon.

The GST Council (Article 279A): Apex federal decision-making body comprising Union Finance Minister (Chair), Union MoS Finance, and Finance Ministers of all States. Decisions require a 75% weighted majority (Centre carries 1/3rd voting weight; all States combined carry 2/3rd voting weight), institutionalizing cooperative fiscal federalism.

Items Outside GST Purview: Crude petroleum, high-speed diesel, motor spirit (petrol), natural gas, aviation turbine fuel (ATF), and alcoholic liquor for human consumption (retained under State excise and VAT).

content.text: Part A: Mains Analytical & Descriptive Questions

items:
Examine the legal challenges encountered in determining the territorial jurisdiction of courts in cyber-crime cases. Discuss the relevant extra-territorial provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Define the borderless, transnational, and anonymous nature of cyberspace conflicting with traditional physical territoriality (Section 177 CrPC); analyze Section 75 of the IT Act (applying to offenses committed outside India by any person if target involves a computer system located in India); detail operational roadblocks: use of darknet, multi-hop proxy VPNs, servers located in hostile foreign jurisdictions, procedural delays in Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLAT), and lack of standardized global cloud data extradition frameworks (e.g., Budapest Convention debate); conclude with reforms: specialized cyber-crime courts, international treaties, and cloud data preservation protocols.

Discuss the significance of the landmark Supreme Court ruling in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015). Why was Section 66A of the IT Act struck down? (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Outline the factual context of Section 66A penalizing 'offensive' electronic messages; analyze grounds for invalidation by a 2-judge bench: (1) Overbreadth and vagueness violating Article 19(1)(a), failing the clear and present danger test, (2) Not protected under reasonable restrictions of Article 19(2), (3) Creating a 'chilling effect' on free speech; highlight how Section 69A (website blocking) was upheld with procedural safeguards; discuss contemporary enforcement issues where police continued invoking the dead section until the SC's 2022 directives.

Analyze the structural advantages and federal friction points of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime in India. (APPSC Group-1 Mains, 10 Marks)
-> Model Approach: Detail economic advantages: elimination of tax cascading via Input Tax Credit, creation of a unified common national market, digitization through GSTN reducing evasion, growth of monthly revenues (>₹1.7 lakh crore); analyze federal friction points: erosion of state fiscal sovereignty (loss of independent sales tax autonomy), dispute over the expiry of the 5-year GST compensation cess window in June 2022, Union veto power in GST Council (holding 33.3% vote where 75% is required); conclude on strengthening dispute resolution and streamlining inverted duty structures.

content.text: Part B: Screening / Prelims Objective Questions

items:
Q1. In which landmark judgment did the Supreme Court of India strike down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 as unconstitutional?
(a) K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India
(b) Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015)
(c) Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India
(d) Common Cause v. Union of India
Correct Answer: (b) Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) [Explanation: In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A for being unconstitutionally vague and violative of the freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).]

Q2. Under the Information Technology Act, 2000, which national agency is designated as the nodal agency for responding to computer security incidents?
(a) National Cyber Coordination Centre (NCCC)
(b) Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In)
(c) National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC)
(d) Defence Cyber Agency (DCA)
Correct Answer: (b) Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) [Explanation: Section 70B of the IT Act designates CERT-In as the national agency for cyber incident response, vulnerability reporting, and emergency coordination.]

Q3. The Goods and Services Tax (GST) was introduced in India by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
(a) 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014
(b) 100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015
(c) 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016
(d) 103rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019
Correct Answer: (c) 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 [Explanation: The 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016 paved the way for the implementation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) nationwide from July 1, 2017.]

Q4. Which of the following commodities is currently EXCLUDED from the levy of Goods and Services Tax (GST) in India?
(a) Natural Gas and Petroleum Products
(b) Textiles and Garments
(c) Motor Vehicles
(d) Mobile Phones and Electronics
Correct Answer: (a) Natural Gas and Petroleum Products [Explanation: Five petroleum products (petrol, diesel, crude, natural gas, ATF) and alcoholic liquor for human consumption remain outside the GST tax ambit, taxed under VAT and State excise.]

Q5. Wealth Tax in India was formally abolished in which Union Budget year and replaced with an additional surcharge on high-income earners?
(a) Union Budget 2012–13
(b) Union Budget 2015–16
(c) Union Budget 2017–18
(d) Union Budget 2020–21
Correct Answer: (b) Union Budget 2015–16 [Explanation: Wealth Tax was abolished in the Union Budget 2015–16 due to high collection costs and replaced with a 2% surcharge on super-rich individuals.]
